body.text: Overview and Empirical Foundations of Factory system

Understanding Factory system gives readers in business an immediate analytical advantage. Instead of relying on vague summaries, this guide breaks down the core mechanics, verified benchmarks, and practical steps.

Most operators overlook how Factory system drives unit economics and competitive moats at scale. Understanding its real-world mechanics reveals why disciplined organizations outperform during market shifts.

The factory system is a method of manufacturing whereby workers and manufacturing equipment are centralized in a factory, the work is supervised and structured through a division of labor, and the manufacturing process is mechanized.

Because of the high capital cost of machinery and factory buildings, factories are typically privately owned by wealthy individuals or corporations who employ the operative labor. Use of machinery with the division of labor reduced the required skill-level of workers and also increased the output per worker.

The factory system was first adopted by successive entrepreneurs in Britain at the beginning of the Industrial Revolution in the late eighteenth century and later spread around the world. It replaced the putting-out system (domestic system).

The main characteristic of the factory system is the use of machinery, originally powered by water or steam and later by electricity. Other characteristics of the system mostly derive from the use of machinery or economies of scale, the centralization of factories, and standardization of interchangeable parts.
